Neural networks as value functions

In Lessons 61 to 63 a person chose the features and only the weights were learned. A neural network learns the features too. Each hidden unit is a feature whose shape and position are trained along with the weights that combine them.

Target
target $v_\pi(s)$ network $\hat v(s,\boldsymbol\theta)$ each unit's term $c_j h_j(s)$
Training steps0
Mean squared error–
Parameters $3H + 1$–

The maths

The network has one input $s$, one layer of $H$ hidden units and one output:

$$h_j(s) = \tanh(a_j s + b_j), \qquad \hat v(s, \boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_{j=1}^{H} c_j\, h_j(s) + d.$$

Each hidden unit is an S-shaped step whose steepness $a_j$ and position $b_j$ are learned. The output is a weighted sum of them, exactly like Lesson 61 but with features that move. $\boldsymbol\theta = (\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}, d)$ holds all $3H + 1$ numbers.

Learning uses the same update as Lesson 62, with $\boldsymbol\theta$ in place of $\mathbf{w}$:

$$\boldsymbol\theta \leftarrow \boldsymbol\theta + \alpha\,\big[U_t - \hat v(S_t, \boldsymbol\theta)\big]\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} \hat v(S_t, \boldsymbol\theta).$$

The gradient comes from the chain rule, using $\tanh'(x) = 1 - \tanh^2(x)$. Computing it layer by layer, output first, is called backpropagation:

$$\frac{\partial \hat v}{\partial d} = 1, \quad \frac{\partial \hat v}{\partial c_j} = h_j, \quad \frac{\partial \hat v}{\partial b_j} = c_j\,(1 - h_j^2), \quad \frac{\partial \hat v}{\partial a_j} = c_j\,(1 - h_j^2)\, s.$$

Unlike the linear case, $\overline{\text{VE}}$ is no longer a bowl. It can have many local minima, so "New random start" can end at different fits. Gradient Monte Carlo still converges to a local minimum. Semi-gradient TD has no such guarantee here (S&B §9.7, §11.3).

With enough hidden units, a network like this can approximate any continuous function on an interval as closely as you like (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991). That says nothing about how much data or training it takes.

To isolate the representation, this demo fits known targets at 101 states at once with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015), a version of gradient descent that scales each parameter's step by a running average of its gradient's size. In RL the targets would be returns or TD targets arriving one at a time.
